groups.title: What is Micronaut and how does it differ from Spring Boot
groups.mechanism: separate build work, startup work and work on every request in your explanation. Use this comparison to open an interview answer, then defend it with a concrete workload: | Dimension | Micronaut | Spring Boot | |---|---|---| | DI and AOP | Generated definitions and interception machinery are central to the design | Conventional runtime discovery/proxies, with a supported AOT path | | HTTP execution | Common Netty setup makes event-loop discipline important | Distinguish servlet MVC from reactive WebFlux before comparing | | Persistence | Choose Data JDBC, JPA or R2DBC deliberately | Choose Spring Data module and persistence backend deliberately | | Native packaging | Requires compatible libraries and a tested native build | Requires compatible libraries, Spring AOT and a tested native build | | Decision evidence | Equivalent readiness, memory, throughput and failure tests | The same measurements and acceptance criteria | The table compares architectural choices; it does not rank frameworks or imply that all applications use these defaults.
groups.tradeOff: potential footprint improvements must pay for migration and ecosystem costs.
groups.verify: profile equivalent services with the same database, payloads, JVM flags and resource limits.

questions.question: What is Micronaut and how does it differ from Spring Boot?
questions.answer: Compare when framework work happens, available integrations and operational fit. Micronaut moves much discovery work into compilation. Conventional Spring applications do more at startup, while Spring also supports AOT. Neither framework choice alone establishes better latency or lower total cost. Micronaut core, Spring AOT.

questions.question: Is Boot a replacement JVM?
questions.answer: no; an ordinary Boot or Micronaut artifact runs on a JVM. Native packaging is a separate choice.

questions.question: Your service spends most time waiting for SQL. Will switching fix latency?
questions.answer: first measure query time, connection waits and network latency; framework startup changes may not affect the bottleneck.

questions.question: What would justify a migration?
questions.answer: a measured deployment constraint and a credible migration benefit after integration, training and support costs.

questions.question: How would you benchmark Micronaut and Spring Boot fairly?
questions.answer: profile equivalent services with the same database, payloads, JVM flags and resource limits.

groups.title: Does compile-time DI mean every dependency is resolved during compilation
groups.mechanism: generated definitions and runtime object creation are different phases. A Micronaut BeanDefinition describes constructor arguments, injected members, qualifiers, scope and lifecycle methods. When a bean is requested, the context uses eligible definitions to resolve its collaborators and construct the scoped object. A definition is not the object itself. See the BeanDefinition API. Walkthrough: an order service needs a payment gateway. Compilation can generate the service's construction metadata without knowing the production endpoint or credentials. At runtime, conditions select the eligible gateway, configuration supplies its endpoint, and construction may still fail. If gateway creation requires the order service in return, there is a dependency cycle; a provider can defer a lookup but does not remove a cycle that is immediately traversed. Prefer moving shared policy into a third dependency over disguising the cycle.
groups.tradeOff: earlier metadata generation makes compiler configuration part of application correctness.
groups.verify: clean-build the artifact in CI and start its context with both valid and deliberately missing dependencies.

questions.question: Does compile-time DI mean every dependency is resolved during compilation?
questions.answer: Micronaut generates bean metadata, then creates objects in an application context. Environment-dependent availability and external resources still matter at runtime. Compilation is one validation boundary, not proof that production can start. DI guide.

questions.question: Why prefer constructor injection?
questions.answer: it makes required collaborators explicit and supports direct unit construction.

questions.question: Two implementations satisfy the same interface. What happens?
questions.answer: define the intended selection with qualifiers or an appropriate primary bean; do not depend on discovery order.

questions.question: How would you diagnose a missing production bean?
questions.answer: inspect generated metadata, packaging, conditions and effective configuration before adding arbitrary scanning settings.

questions.question: How would you test a generated dependency graph?
questions.answer: clean-build the artifact in CI and start its context with both valid and deliberately missing dependencies.

groups.title: How do the common Spring and Micronaut annotations map
groups.mechanism: annotations only work when their supporting processor or runtime integration recognizes them.
groups.tradeOff: compatibility modules can ease transition but expand the behavior matrix to verify.
groups.verify: assert bean selection, lifecycle and HTTP results through the actual context, rather than checking annotation text.

questions.question: How do the common Spring and Micronaut annotations map?
questions.answer: Translate the contract, not just the annotation name. Check scope, imports, route behavior, validation and test lifecycle. A compiler accepting an annotation is not proof the selected framework processes it. Micronaut core reference.

questions.question: Are the two ConfigurationProperties annotations the same type?
questions.answer: no; the simple names match but the packages and binding contracts differ.

questions.question: A factory creates a vendor SDK client. Who closes it?
questions.answer: specify ownership and the supported destruction hook; avoid leaked pools and duplicate clients.

questions.question: How do you review a bulk annotation conversion?
questions.answer: inventory observable contracts and migrate one tested boundary at a time.

questions.question: How would you verify an annotation migration?
questions.answer: assert bean selection, lifecycle and HTTP results through the actual context, rather than checking annotation text.

groups.title: Is Micronaut always faster and smaller than Spring Boot
groups.mechanism: class loading, initialization, JIT compilation and dependency setup affect different phases.
groups.tradeOff: optimize for the workload's constraints rather than one headline number.
groups.verify: publish a reproducible workload, error rate, repetitions and confidence range alongside resource usage.

questions.question: Is Micronaut always faster and smaller than Spring Boot?
questions.answer: There is no universal winner. Benchmark the actual workload, including dependencies, warm-up, container limits and JVM versus native mode. Use repeated measurements and an explicit target such as time to the first successful business request. Framework labels are not benchmark results.

questions.question: Is a startup log line a readiness measurement?
questions.answer: not necessarily; required pools, migrations or remote dependencies may still be unavailable.

questions.question: One service has security enabled and the other does not. Is the comparison fair?
questions.answer: no; equalize behavior and dependencies before interpreting results.

questions.question: How do you compare scale-to-zero economics?
questions.answer: include cold starts, build cost, minimum instances, burst behavior and cost per successful request.

questions.question: How would you measure cold and warm service behavior?
questions.answer: publish a reproducible workload, error rate, repetitions and confidence range alongside resource usage.

groups.title: How do scopes and lifecycle differ from thread safety
groups.mechanism: the container manages object ownership; the application manages safe state transitions. In the baseline Micronaut container, singleton definitions are normally lazy; @Context requests initialization with the context. Application builders or generated application configuration can enable eager initialization, so inspect the actual startup configuration. Conventional Spring singleton startup is typically eager unless lazy behavior is configured. Micronaut Context scope. Construction, dependency injection, @PostConstruct and eventual @PreDestroy represent different lifecycle stages. Keep initialization bounded and define what must succeed before readiness. For example, validate a required endpoint before traffic, but avoid making every optional cache warm-up a reason to restart the service. Do not assume shutdown callbacks run after an abrupt process kill; durable work needs recovery on the next start.
groups.tradeOff: shared reusable clients reduce allocations but require correct lifecycle and concurrent use.
groups.verify: overlap requests for different identities, then close the context while work is pending and assert bounded cleanup.

questions.question: How do scopes and lifecycle differ from thread safety?
questions.answer: Scope is not synchronization. Keep shared services stateless when practical, and make request identity explicit. A prototype injected once into a singleton does not automatically become a fresh object on each method call; use an appropriate provider or scope boundary.

questions.question: Can a singleton hold the current customer's ID?
questions.answer: a mutable field would mix concurrent users; pass identity explicitly or use supported request context.

questions.question: Why did a lazy dependency fail only on the first request?
questions.answer: context creation did not exercise its construction path; readiness needs deliberate coverage.

questions.question: What changes during shutdown with requests in flight?
questions.answer: coordinate admission, bounded draining and resource closure; cancellation may be cooperative.

questions.question: How would you test scope isolation and shutdown?
questions.answer: overlap requests for different identities, then close the context while work is pending and assert bounded cleanup.

groups.title: How do conditions and configuration replace Boot auto-configuration
groups.mechanism: conditional availability and value binding are separate checks. Diagnose configuration in order: which sources are present, which source wins for a key, whether conversion succeeds, whether validation succeeds, and which beans become eligible. A property name copied from Boot has no effect unless Micronaut or application code binds it. Walkthrough: a packaged default says the gateway is disabled, but deployment configuration enables it and supplies a blank endpoint. The correct result is an explicit invalid-configuration failure before traffic, not silent fallback to a fake implementation. Record the selected mode and safe source information in diagnostics without logging credentials. Prove precedence with an isolated test containing two conflicting values; avoid memorizing one framework's source order and applying it to the other.
groups.tradeOff: flexible defaults reduce setup effort but can hide unsafe deployment states.
groups.verify: start contexts with a configuration matrix and assert the selected implementation and failure message without exposing secrets.

questions.question: How do conditions and configuration replace Boot auto-configuration?
questions.answer: Define explicit defaults and typed configuration, then validate invariants before accepting traffic. Test missing, empty and conflicting settings. Treat feature-off and integration-misconfigured as separate states; silently falling back can send traffic to the wrong destination.

questions.question: Is a missing value equivalent to an empty string?
questions.answer: not generally; binding, defaults and validation determine the result.

questions.question: Why does a test obtain a fake gateway in production mode?
questions.answer: inspect environment activation, conditions and replacement rules; ensure the fake cannot satisfy production wiring.

questions.question: Does changing a property refresh every existing singleton?
questions.answer: do not assume dynamic rebinding; define supported refresh scope and in-flight behavior explicitly.

questions.question: How would you test conditional configuration combinations?
questions.answer: start contexts with a configuration matrix and assert the selected implementation and failure message without exposing secrets.

groups.title: How does Micronaut AOP differ from Spring proxy AOP
groups.mechanism: default Micronaut around advice subclasses the target and invokes the original method through a super call; proxy-target mode delegates differently. The interceptor chain is selected from advice metadata, and each interceptor can proceed, alter the result or fail the call. Private methods cannot be overridden; final classes or methods constrain subclass advice. Constructor execution is not an ordinary advised method call. Call-path exercise: with supported default subclass advice, an external call to an advised method and an eligible virtual self-call can enter the interception chain. With ordinary Spring proxy AOP, a self-call on the target bypasses the external proxy. Neither statement grants advice to an object created with new, and neither replaces checking the actual annotation's proxy configuration. For a retrying transaction, sketch the chain explicitly: retry outside transaction can create a fresh transaction per attempt; transaction outside retry can reuse a transaction already marked rollback-only.
groups.tradeOff: generated interception shifts constraints to compilation but does not remove invocation semantics.
groups.verify: call through the container, count actual interceptor executions for external and internal calls, and test the selected mode.

questions.question: How does Micronaut AOP differ from Spring proxy AOP?
questions.answer: Spring proxy self-invocation normally bypasses advice. Micronaut's default subclass-based around advice can intercept eligible calls from within the class, while proxy-target configurations differ. Avoid copying either rule universally. Verify the concrete advice, method visibility and generated proxy mode.

questions.question: Does manually constructing the service preserve advice?
questions.answer: ordinary direct construction bypasses container-provided interception.

questions.question: Does a private helper become transactional just by adding an annotation?
questions.answer: private methods cannot be overridden by a subclass proxy; put the boundary on a supported entry point.

questions.question: Why can retry and transaction ordering change outcomes?
questions.answer: retries inside a failed transaction differ from fresh transactions per attempt; determine interceptor order and prove rollback behavior.

questions.question: How would you prove which calls actually receive advice?
questions.answer: call through the container, count actual interceptor executions for external and internal calls, and test the selected mode.

groups.title: Why must blocking work leave the HTTP event loop
groups.mechanism: distinguish request dispatch, blocking execution and response completion threads. @ExecuteOn selects a named executor boundary; it does not turn the underlying database driver into a nonblocking driver. Also inspect filters and client callbacks: moving a controller does not automatically make unrelated earlier or later blocking work safe. Capacity exercise: a service has a pool of 20 database connections. Offloading 2,000 requests to workers or virtual threads cannot produce 2,000 simultaneous database operations. Most requests wait for a connection. Limit admitted work, bound acquisition time and leave enough end-to-end budget to execute the query and return the response. Otherwise the event loop remains responsive while user requests still expire in a hidden queue.
groups.tradeOff: offloading protects multiplexing but introduces queues and context propagation boundaries.
groups.verify: inject database latency and inspect event-loop stacks, queue depth, health latency and rejected requests.

questions.question: Why must blocking work leave the HTTP event loop?
questions.answer: In Micronaut, use an appropriate executor boundary such as ExecuteOn for blocking work and confirm the configured thread-selection policy. Moving work off the event loop still needs bounded concurrency, timeouts and rejection behavior. A reactive return type alone does not make JDBC nonblocking.

questions.question: Is Thread.sleep safe on an event loop?
questions.answer: it blocks that thread and delays unrelated connections.

questions.question: Does wrapping a blocking call in a publisher fix it?
questions.answer: only if execution actually moves to an appropriate scheduler; creation and subscription location matter.

questions.question: Will an unlimited worker pool solve overload?
questions.answer: it can amplify pressure on the database; align admission and concurrency with downstream capacity.

questions.question: How would you detect blocking work on an event loop?
questions.answer: inject database latency and inspect event-loop stacks, queue depth, health latency and rejected requests.

groups.title: How do you migrate REST binding, validation and errors
groups.mechanism: binding failures can occur before the service or its local error-handling code runs.
groups.tradeOff: centralized mapping improves consistency but must preserve domain-specific distinctions.
groups.verify: replay a golden set of valid and invalid requests against both implementations and compare status, headers and JSON.

questions.question: How do you migrate REST binding, validation and errors?
questions.answer: Preserve observable behavior with request fixtures. Test missing fields, explicit null, malformed JSON and unsupported content types. Use framework validation and error handling intentionally, and expose stable safe error codes rather than exception internals. Micronaut HTTP reference.

questions.question: Is an absent request body the same as an empty object?
questions.answer: no; binding and validation can reject them at different stages.

questions.question: An entity is absent. Should the API return an empty successful object?
questions.answer: follow the published absence contract, commonly a deliberate 404; do not let framework defaults decide accidentally.

questions.question: How do you avoid leaking SQL details on failure?
questions.answer: map exceptions to safe errors, log restricted diagnostics with correlation IDs, and test negative responses.

questions.question: How would you compare old and new REST error contracts?
questions.answer: replay a golden set of valid and invalid requests against both implementations and compare status, headers and JSON.

groups.title: How do declarative clients, retries and cancellation interact
groups.mechanism: connection acquisition, connection establishment and response waiting consume different portions of the budget.
groups.tradeOff: retries improve transient availability while increasing load and outcome ambiguity.
groups.verify: delay a response after the server commits, cancel the caller and repeat the key; assert one business effect.

questions.question: How do declarative clients, retries and cancellation interact?
questions.answer: Specify deadlines, connection limits, retryable failures and idempotency independently of client syntax. A lost response can leave the remote action committed. Local cancellation or a timeout does not prove the remote work stopped. Reconcile unknown outcomes before retrying writes.

questions.question: Is every 500 safe to retry?
questions.answer: no; determine operation semantics and whether side effects may already have occurred.

questions.question: A payment times out after submission. What next?
questions.answer: reuse an idempotency key and query the operation state according to the provider contract.

questions.question: How do nested retries amplify traffic?
questions.answer: attempts multiply across layers; allocate one end-to-end deadline and a controlled retry budget.

questions.question: How would you test an HTTP timeout after remote commit?
questions.answer: delay a response after the server commits, cancel the caller and repeat the key; assert one business effect.

groups.title: How does Micronaut Data differ from Spring Data
groups.mechanism: query generation, parameter binding, execution and result mapping are separate stages.
groups.tradeOff: earlier repository validation improves feedback without replacing database integration tests.
groups.verify: run migrations and repository tests on the target database, including empty results, duplicates and boundary pages.

questions.question: How does Micronaut Data differ from Spring Data?
questions.answer: Compare repository generation separately from the storage backend. Micronaut Data JDBC, JPA and R2DBC have different persistence and execution models. Porting a repository method name does not establish equivalent SQL, pagination, transaction or locking behavior.

questions.question: Can compilation detect every bad production query?
questions.answer: no; permissions, schema drift, data distribution and vendor behavior remain runtime concerns.

questions.question: Why does pagination become unstable?
questions.answer: missing deterministic ordering or concurrent changes can repeat or omit rows; define stable ordering and pagination semantics.

questions.question: How do you review a dialect migration?
questions.answer: inspect generated SQL and real query plans with production-like volumes and the intended database version.

questions.question: How would you validate generated repository SQL?
questions.answer: run migrations and repository tests on the target database, including empty results, duplicates and boundary pages.

groups.title: Can you replace Hibernate with JDBC by changing a dependency
groups.mechanism: object identity inside a persistence context is different from repeated row mapping.
groups.tradeOff: explicit SQL behavior can improve predictability but increases responsibility for aggregate persistence.
groups.verify: reload from a separate transaction, test competing writers and assert query counts for relationships.

questions.question: Can you replace Hibernate with JDBC by changing a dependency?
questions.answer: A JPA-to-JDBC migration changes the persistence model. Make writes and relationship fetching explicit, preserve optimistic locking and test aggregate boundaries. Keeping Micronaut Data JPA initially can reduce the number of simultaneous changes.

questions.question: Does modifying a loaded object necessarily update a JDBC row?
questions.answer: no; issue an explicit supported update rather than assuming dirty checking.

questions.question: How can an endpoint lose nested data?
questions.answer: previous lazy access or fetch configuration may no longer apply; define the required projection or join.

questions.question: Two requests update the same version. What must remain true?
questions.answer: use an atomic version predicate and surface a conflict instead of silently losing one update.

questions.question: How would you prove a JDBC update is persisted?
questions.answer: reload from a separate transaction, test competing writers and assert query counts for relationships.

groups.title: What must you verify about transactions and async boundaries
groups.mechanism: transaction ownership and completion must follow the chosen imperative or reactive execution model. For an imperative transaction, identify the manager and connection that own the work. For a reactive transaction, identify the subscription and supported context carrying it. Merely returning a future or publisher does not establish that all deferred work is enclosed in the transaction. Failure walkthrough: an order transaction inserts an order and publishes an HTTP notification. If the notification succeeds and the database rolls back, the receiver has observed an order that does not exist. Reversing the order leaves the opposite gap after commit. An outbox stores the order and publication intent atomically in one database transaction, then publishes with retries. The publisher can crash after sending but before marking completion, so consumers must tolerate duplicates; the annotation cannot provide cross-system exactly-once behavior.
groups.tradeOff: short transactions reduce locking but require deliberate coordination with external effects.
groups.verify: force failures before and after commit, inspect durable rows, and redeliver events concurrently.

questions.question: What must you verify about transactions and async boundaries?
questions.answer: Verify manager selection, propagation, rollback rules and the real interception path. Do not assume an arbitrary executor task inherits a thread-bound transaction. For reactive access, use supported reactive transaction context rather than transferring a JDBC connection across threads.

questions.question: If an exception is caught, will rollback always happen?
questions.answer: no; inspect rollback-only state and the actual transaction contract, including checked exceptions.

questions.question: The database commits but event publication fails. What now?
questions.answer: use an outbox or another explicit recovery protocol, with duplicate-safe consumption.

questions.question: Can retrying a transaction repeat external effects?
questions.answer: yes; exclude irreversible effects from retried transaction bodies or give them durable idempotency semantics.

questions.question: How would you test transaction failure boundaries?
questions.answer: force failures before and after commit, inspect durable rows, and redeliver events concurrently.

groups.title: What is the difference between introspection and serialization
groups.mechanism: generated metadata and wire-format policy solve different problems.
groups.tradeOff: compile-time serialization constrains dynamic use but can make supported types explicit.
groups.verify: test golden JSON, unknown fields, omitted fields, nulls and round trips through the selected serializer.

questions.question: What is the difference between introspection and serialization?
questions.answer: Identify whether the service uses Micronaut Serialization or Jackson Databind, then configure DTO support for that integration. Preserve field names, null rules, date formats and allowed inputs. Avoid exposing persistence entities as accidental public schemas.

questions.question: Does a Java field rename preserve its JSON name?
questions.answer: only if the explicit mapping or serializer contract preserves it.

questions.question: What if an older caller omits a newly required field?
questions.answer: define compatibility behavior; avoid silently assigning a value that changes business meaning.

questions.question: How do you prevent a request from setting administrative fields?
questions.answer: use explicit input DTOs and authorization; serializer configuration alone is not an access-control boundary.

questions.question: How would you test JSON compatibility across serializers?
questions.answer: test golden JSON, unknown fields, omitted fields, nulls and round trips through the selected serializer.

groups.title: How do you migrate authentication and authorization safely
groups.mechanism: route matching, identity validation and resource policy are separate decisions.
groups.tradeOff: centralized policies simplify audit but can miss object-level rules without explicit service checks.
groups.verify: exercise anonymous, expired, wrong-audience, wrong-tenant and insufficient-role requests, including error paths.

questions.question: How do you migrate authentication and authorization safely?
questions.answer: Recreate security requirements explicitly instead of copying filter configuration. Validate trusted token issuer, audience, signature and time claims, then enforce resource ownership and tenant boundaries. Preserve public-route exceptions deliberately and protect operational endpoints.

questions.question: Does decoding a JWT authenticate the caller?
questions.answer: no; parsing claims does not verify trust or validity.

questions.question: An authenticated user requests another customer's order. Is a role enough?
questions.answer: check resource ownership and tenant isolation in addition to coarse roles.

questions.question: What happens during signing-key rotation?
questions.answer: test trusted-key refresh, overlap and unknown key behavior; never accept arbitrary token-provided key URLs.

questions.question: How would you test tenant-aware security enforcement?
questions.answer: exercise anonymous, expired, wrong-audience, wrong-tenant and insufficient-role requests, including error paths.

groups.title: How does MicronautTest differ from a plain unit test
groups.mechanism: test context, server request and database transaction can have different lifetimes.
groups.tradeOff: isolation improves repeatability, while realistic integrations reveal more boundary failures.
groups.verify: run tests independently and in parallel, assert committed state from another connection, and use deterministic cleanup.

questions.question: How does MicronautTest differ from a plain unit test?
questions.answer: Use unit tests for business decisions, context tests for wiring and advice, HTTP tests for the API, and real database tests for persistence. A test-managed transaction does not imply a separately executed server request shares it. Verify cleanup and commit behavior explicitly.

questions.question: Can direct construction test AOP?
questions.answer: it tests the object logic but bypasses container interception.

questions.question: Why does a mocked repository hide a transaction bug?
questions.answer: it may return values without enforcing actual commit, locking or constraint semantics.

questions.question: How do you prevent test configuration masking production wiring?
questions.answer: keep a packaged-artifact smoke test with production-like conditions and assert which integrations are selected.

questions.question: How would you detect integration-test cleanup leakage?
questions.answer: run tests independently and in parallel, assert committed state from another connection, and use deterministic cleanup.

groups.title: What can go wrong with annotation processing and multi-module builds
groups.mechanism: generation, compilation and packaging are distinct stages; each can drop required outputs.
groups.tradeOff: compile-time work reduces discovery overhead but makes artifact provenance essential.
groups.verify: consume the published library in a minimal clean application and start its context without local build outputs.

questions.question: What can go wrong with annotation processing and multi-module builds?
questions.answer: Treat processors, generated resources and platform alignment as build inputs. Reproduce failures with a clean command-line build, inspect the published library, and compare IDE and CI configuration. Compile success without the needed processor can still produce an unusable application artifact.

questions.question: Why can incremental compilation hide a problem?
questions.answer: old generated files can survive and satisfy a local run.

questions.question: A bean works in its module but disappears after publication. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: inspect the actual JAR, metadata, package processing rules and dependency scopes.

questions.question: How do you keep processors compatible with runtime libraries?
questions.answer: use the matching platform and build plugins, inspect the resolved graph and avoid independent arbitrary version overrides.

questions.question: How would you verify a published bean-library artifact?
questions.answer: consume the published library in a minimal clean application and start its context without local build outputs.

groups.title: How do Micronaut and Spring Boot compare for GraalVM native images
groups.mechanism: framework AOT generation and the native-image compiler are related but separate build stages.
groups.tradeOff: startup or memory gains can be offset by build cost and observability limitations.
groups.verify: exercise security, serialization, TLS, resource loading and database paths in the native artifact under target container limits.

questions.question: How do Micronaut and Spring Boot compare for GraalVM native images?
questions.answer: Treat JVM and native packaging as separate targets. Check reflection, resources, proxies, initialization and library support. Compare cold readiness, memory and warmed throughput against longer builds and different diagnostics. Run the actual native executable before approving it.

questions.question: Does a passing JVM test prove native behavior?
questions.answer: no; reachability and initialization constraints differ.

questions.question: A class loaded by name works on the JVM but fails natively. Why?
questions.answer: dynamic access may need explicit reachability metadata or a different supported integration.

questions.question: What configuration must be varied during verification?
questions.answer: distinguish decisions fixed during AOT processing from supported runtime inputs and test every deployment mode you intend to ship.

questions.question: How would you test the actual native executable?
questions.answer: exercise security, serialization, TLS, resource loading and database paths in the native artifact under target container limits.

groups.title: How do you diagnose a Micronaut service that is healthy but slow
groups.mechanism: a thread transition can separate logging or tracing context from the request unless supported propagation is used.
groups.tradeOff: richer diagnostics cost CPU, memory and storage; sample with sufficient error visibility.
groups.verify: inject latency and pool exhaustion, cancel requests, then confirm traces explain queue time and resources return to baseline.

questions.question: How do you diagnose a Micronaut service that is healthy but slow?
questions.answer: Start with the user-visible SLO and a latency breakdown. Correlate traces with event-loop stalls, worker queues, connection waits, GC and downstream timing. Check that request identity survives executor changes. Keep metric labels bounded and exclude secrets from logs.

questions.question: Why can average latency hide a problem?
questions.answer: a small fraction of very slow requests can violate a p99 target while the average looks acceptable.

questions.question: Should readiness fail whenever an optional dependency slows down?
questions.answer: define capability and dependency policy; removing every instance may worsen an outage.

questions.question: What happens when clients disconnect but expensive work continues?
questions.answer: cancellation may not stop I/O; bound server work with deadlines and admission, and observe abandoned operations.

questions.question: How would you diagnose capacity under cancelled requests?
questions.answer: inject latency and pool exhaustion, cancel requests, then confirm traces explain queue time and resources return to baseline.

groups.title: How would you decide whether to migrate a Spring Boot service to Micronaut
groups.mechanism: build an evidence matrix for bean selection, advice, HTTP errors, JSON, transactions, security, deadlines and shutdown.
groups.tradeOff: migration benefits compete with engineering effort, ecosystem gaps and long-term ownership.
groups.verify: run contract fixtures and failure injection on both artifacts, canary with explicit stop thresholds, and rehearse rollback before expanding traffic.

questions.question: How would you decide whether to migrate a Spring Boot service to Micronaut?
questions.answer: Keep the framework if it meets the requirements economically. Prototype a representative slice if startup, memory or deployment density is a measured constraint. Preserve API, security, data and failure semantics, compare equivalent workloads, and migrate gradually with a tested rollback path.

questions.question: What belongs in the first prototype?
questions.answer: a realistic authenticated endpoint with serialization, database access and one downstream call, not only hello-world.

questions.question: Can shadow traffic safely include write requests?
questions.answer: not against shared side-effecting systems; isolate writes or replay sanitized fixtures into controlled dependencies.

questions.question: How can rollback fail despite routing traffic back?
questions.answer: incompatible schema changes, new persisted states or emitted events may remain; use expand-contract changes and backward-compatible readers.

questions.question: How would you rehearse a framework migration rollback?
questions.answer: run contract fixtures and failure injection on both artifacts, canary with explicit stop thresholds, and rehearse rollback before expanding traffic.

groups.title: How do Named, Primary, Replaces and Factory solve different problems
groups.mechanism: registration, conditional eligibility, replacement and candidate selection jointly determine the result. Describe them as separate concerns without depending on undocumented implementation order. The factory's own lifetime is not a substitute for specifying the produced client's scope and cleanup. Returning a newly allocated client on each lookup can create extra connection pools even when its factory is shared.
groups.tradeOff: defaults reduce injection annotations but can obscure intent. Explicit qualifiers improve auditability at the cost of a more visible wiring contract.
groups.verify: resolve default and named gateways in separate production-like and test contexts. Assert exact candidate counts, selected identities and client closure, including missing and conflicting configurations.

questions.question: How do Named, Primary, Replaces and Factory solve different problems?
questions.answer: Use a qualifier for explicit selection, Primary for a deliberate default, Replaces for an intentional implementation substitution, and Factory for construction. Do not use Primary to hide two accidentally active production gateways. A replacement must target the correct type, qualifier and factory where relevant. Primary API, Replaces API, Factory API.

questions.question: Does Primary delete the other implementation?
questions.answer: no; it expresses selection preference. Another qualified injection can still use the other bean. Multiple primary candidates can still be ambiguous.

questions.question: A test replaces the default gateway, but requests still reach the live gateway. Why?
questions.answer: inspect the injection qualifier and the replacement target. A named factory-produced bean may not match the replacement you intended. Confirm which object the controller actually receives and prevent external traffic in the test environment.

questions.question: Should production fallback use the sandbox gateway when the live bean is unavailable?
questions.answer: no, unless that is a deliberately safe business contract. Missing required production wiring should fail clearly. Fallback is a runtime business decision, not merely a convenient way to satisfy DI.

questions.question: How would you verify qualified bean replacement?
questions.answer: resolve default and named gateways in separate production-like and test contexts. Assert exact candidate counts, selected identities and client closure, including missing and conflicting configurations.

groups.title: When should you use EachProperty and EachBean
groups.mechanism: map entry names normally become named qualifiers; the derived bean inherits the parent's qualifier. List binding is a separate option and requires its own identity reasoning. A deployment configuration update is not proof that existing singleton clients are replaced safely or that old resources are closed.
groups.tradeOff: generated families remove repetitive factories but make configuration cardinality an operational concern. Large, frequently changing tenant populations may need an explicit registry with admission and lifecycle management.
groups.verify: test zero, one and multiple entries; unknown names; invalid entries; exact qualifier-to-client mapping; and total resource limits. On shutdown, verify every initialized client is closed once.

questions.question: When should you use EachProperty and EachBean?
questions.answer: EachProperty models repeated typed configuration, while EachBean derives another bean for each matching parent. Named qualification links each configured entry to its client. Validate every entry and budget total resources. This is useful for a bounded set of integrations, but it is not automatically a dynamic tenant provisioning system.

questions.question: How do you choose the Europe client?
questions.answer: use its explicit qualifier or a controlled selection layer; do not take the first element of an unordered collection.

questions.question: One of three entries has a blank endpoint. Should the other two make the deployment look healthy?
questions.answer: decide whether all configured entries are required. If they are, validate the whole family before readiness rather than discovering one invalid lazy client on its first request.

questions.question: What happens if 500 entries each create a pool of 20 connections?
questions.answer: that permits up to 10,000 connections. Budget resources across all clients, consider shared transport where supported, and bound the configured set.

questions.question: How would you validate all configured client instances?
questions.answer: test zero, one and multiple entries; unknown names; invalid entries; exact qualifier-to-client mapping; and total resource limits. On shutdown, verify every initialized client is closed once.

groups.title: How do Micronaut HTTP filters differ from Spring servlet filters and interceptors
groups.mechanism: the continuation represents downstream work. Calling a blocking continuation can occupy an event-loop thread; asynchronous return types have different continuation and subscription semantics. The HTTP filter chain is distinct from method AOP, so a controller annotation does not establish the behavior of an earlier filter.
groups.tradeOff: centralized request policy improves consistency, but ordering and short-circuit behavior can affect security, diagnostics and latency simultaneously.
groups.verify: record controller invocation count for allowed and rejected requests, test every response path, inject audit latency, and assert headers and safe errors without reading unbounded bodies.

questions.question: How do Micronaut HTTP filters differ from Spring servlet filters and interceptors?
questions.answer: Port the filter's purpose, matching rules, ordering and execution model. Define whether it continues or short-circuits the request and which response paths it observes. A blocking continuation requires appropriate offloading. Route-specific parameters can also change which requests match the filter. RequestFilter API.

questions.question: If a filter returns an unauthorized response, should it also call the continuation?
questions.answer: no; choose rejection or downstream execution for that request. Accidentally doing both can run side effects despite a rejected response.

questions.question: Why does the correlation header disappear on a 404?
questions.answer: inspect route-dependent parameters and matching. A filter that requires a route match may not run for unmatched routes. Test 404, preflight, static-resource and exception paths explicitly.

questions.question: Is logging the entire request body safe?
questions.answer: body access can buffer large streams, alter consumption behavior or expose secrets. Prefer bounded metadata and redact sensitive fields; do not copy authentication headers into logs.

questions.question: How would you verify filter rejection and continuation?
questions.answer: record controller invocation count for allowed and rejected requests, test every response path, inject audit latency, and assert headers and safe errors without reading unbounded bodies.

groups.title: How do reactive demand and Java virtual threads change the execution model
groups.mechanism: a virtual thread still runs on a carrier when executing CPU work. It can unmount during supported waits, which improves concurrency rather than speeding up instructions. Reactive subscription controls when deferred work begins; cancellation requests termination but does not undo a committed effect. TaskExecutors.BLOCKING can use virtual threads when available, with a fallback described by the selected Micronaut version. TaskExecutors API.
groups.tradeOff: virtual threads favor familiar sequential code; reactive pipelines can express streaming demand well but require careful operator and context reasoning.
groups.verify: use slow consumers, duplicate subscriptions and cancellation; inspect active database work, buffered data and retained tasks. For virtual threads, measure pinning and memory under the actual Java 21 runtime.

questions.question: How do reactive demand and Java virtual threads change the execution model?
questions.answer: Choose one understandable execution model per boundary. Reactive demand can regulate compatible streams, while virtual threads simplify high-concurrency blocking code. Both still need bounded admission, connection limits and deadlines. In Micronaut, inspect the actual executor behind the blocking boundary rather than assuming every request uses virtual threads.

questions.question: Does subscribing twice to a cold operation necessarily reuse one result?
questions.answer: no; a cold publisher can execute its source work for each subscription. Repeated subscriptions to a write can repeat side effects unless the operation or sharing strategy prevents that.

questions.question: A stream requests ten rows but the source loads a million into a list. Is memory bounded?
questions.answer: not by downstream demand alone. Source materialization, buffering, prefetch and concurrent mapping must also be bounded.

questions.question: Do virtual threads eliminate Java 21 pinning and ThreadLocal risks?
questions.answer: no. Blocking inside certain synchronized or native operations can pin carriers in Java 21, and per-thread objects can become expensive at high concurrency. Check the exact JDK; newer versions change pinning behavior.

questions.question: How would you test demand, cancellation and virtual-thread capacity?
questions.answer: use slow consumers, duplicate subscriptions and cancellation; inspect active database work, buffered data and retained tasks. For virtual threads, measure pinning and memory under the actual Java 21 runtime.

groups.title: How are retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks different
groups.mechanism: distinguish closed, open and recovery-probe behavior. In the cited Micronaut API, reset controls transition to half-open for a retry. Circuit state is not automatically a cluster-wide signal. With many instances, simultaneous recovery attempts can still load the dependency. A retry delay is also not a substitute for a hard timeout on one stuck network call.
groups.tradeOff: resilience improves availability only when it preserves business truth and fits the downstream's recovery capacity.
groups.verify: deterministically trigger selected failures and recovery, count actual attempts and concurrent calls, and assert fallback semantics. Include a hung call, an excluded error and an ambiguous committed write.

questions.question: How are retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks different?
questions.answer: Give each mechanism a separate contract. Micronaut CircuitBreaker builds on Retryable and maintains circuit state; it does not replace transport deadlines, concurrency limits or idempotency. Define retryable exceptions, recovery behavior and the business meaning of fallback data. CircuitBreaker API.

questions.question: Does an open circuit stop calls already executing?
questions.answer: do not assume it cancels in-flight work. Existing calls still need their own deadlines and cleanup; new calls follow the open-circuit policy.

questions.question: Three layers each allow one initial call and two retries. What is the worst-case amplification?
questions.answer: three attempts per layer can produce 27 downstream attempts for one original request. Count total attempts explicitly rather than ambiguously saying “three retries.”

questions.question: Should a fallback report successful payment when the provider is unreachable?
questions.answer: no. Return a truthful unavailable or pending/unknown outcome according to the payment contract, then reconcile. A fallback must not manufacture business success.

questions.question: How would you validate circuit recovery and retry counts?
questions.answer: deterministically trigger selected failures and recovery, count actual attempts and concurrent calls, and assert fallback semantics. Include a hung call, an excluded error and an ambiguous committed write.

groups.title: Are application events and Scheduled jobs durable or cluster-wide
groups.mechanism: publishEvent publishes synchronously; publishEventAsync returns a future for asynchronous publication. Listener-level asynchronous work can add another completion boundary. Neither API persists the event for replay after process loss. ApplicationEventPublisher API. For scheduling, there are three different completions: the scheduler invokes a method, that method may submit work, and the work later commits an effect. Track the right one. Cron evaluated in a local default time zone can behave unexpectedly around daylight-saving changes; define the zone and the treatment of repeated or missing business periods.
groups.tradeOff: local scheduling is simple for best-effort housekeeping. Durable orchestration adds storage and coordination but makes ownership and recovery explicit.
groups.verify: run two instances, interrupt a run before and after the effect, expire ownership and restart. Assert one business effect per durable job key and recoverable status for unfinished work.

questions.question: Are application events and Scheduled jobs durable or cluster-wide?
questions.answer: Separate in-process notification from durable work. A scheduled invoice job on three replicas can execute three times. Use durable job identity, idempotent effects and an appropriate ownership protocol when completion must survive crashes. Specify time zone, overlap policy, deadlines and failure reporting.

questions.question: What is the difference between fixed delay and fixed rate?
questions.answer: fixed delay measures the gap after completion; fixed rate targets a cadence. Do not infer overlap guarantees for work that the method hands off asynchronously. Scheduling invocation completion is not necessarily business-work completion.

questions.question: You begin publishing an in-process event after committing an order, then crash before listeners finish. Is delivery guaranteed?
questions.answer: no durable delivery follows from publication alone. Persist an outbox or job record with the order when notification must survive failure. For synchronous listeners, also consider whether listener failure propagates to the publisher; asynchronous listeners change where failure is observed.

questions.question: A lease expires while the old worker is still running. Is the new worker the only writer?
questions.answer: no; the old worker may continue. Use a fencing token or another storage-enforced ownership check where needed, plus an idempotency constraint on the business effect.

questions.question: How would you test scheduled work across replicas?
questions.answer: run two instances, interrupt a run before and after the effect, expire ownership and restart. Assert one business effect per durable job key and recoverable status for unfinished work.

groups.title: What changes when migrating Spring cache annotations to Micronaut Cache
groups.mechanism: cache correctness combines interception with key generation and provider semantics. An absent value, a cached “not found” result and a failed load are different states. A short negative TTL can reduce repeated misses, but long retention can hide newly created data. For bounded age, distinguish expiry after write from expiry after access: a frequently accessed stale value can survive indefinitely under access-based expiry alone. Even write-based expiry needs a policy for stale reloads and post-commit invalidation races. Memory bounds additionally require size or weight limits. Caffeine eviction policies.
groups.tradeOff: caching reduces dependency load while introducing staleness and invalidation work. Distributed caches share state but add network and availability concerns.
groups.verify: compare cross-tenant keys, missing-versus-created records, concurrent misses, rollback and post-commit invalidation failures. Measure both stale-read duration and actual backend load, with two instances when sharing matters.

questions.question: What changes when migrating Spring cache annotations to Micronaut Cache?
questions.answer: Preserve the cache contract: key, value shape, tenant boundary, expiry, maximum size, negative-result policy and invalidation timing. Determine whether storage is local or shared and whether calls actually cross the advice boundary. Never treat a cache hit as authorization by itself.

questions.question: Is product ID alone a safe key for tenant-specific prices?
questions.answer: no. Include every input affecting the result, such as tenant, currency and applicable pricing version, or separate the caches deliberately.

questions.question: A database update rolls back after the cache was updated. What does the next reader see?
questions.answer: potentially uncommitted data. Coordinate cache change with successful commit and define recovery for failed invalidation. Local transaction rollback does not automatically undo a separate cache write.

questions.question: Does a local single-flight loader prevent a stampede across 50 replicas?
questions.answer: not necessarily; each replica can perform its own load. Decide whether that aggregate load is acceptable before adding shared coordination, and keep loaders safe to repeat.

questions.question: How would you test cache consistency after transaction rollback?
questions.answer: compare cross-tenant keys, missing-versus-created records, concurrent misses, rollback and post-commit invalidation failures. Measure both stale-read duration and actual backend load, with two instances when sharing matters.

groups.title: How do Kafka listener acknowledgments interact with database commits
groups.mechanism: subscription ownership, handler completion, database commit and offset commit are four distinct events. For database idempotency, atomically record the operation key and apply the effect. Redelivery can then recognize the committed operation. Poison records need an explicit retry/quarantine policy; moving a record aside is itself an operation whose failure and acknowledgment ordering must be handled.
groups.tradeOff: ordered processing simplifies progress reasoning but can let a slow record block a partition. Parallel processing requires stronger completion tracking and resource limits.
groups.verify: stop the consumer before the effect, after commit and before acknowledgment; force reassignment; redeliver duplicates concurrently; and inject a poison record. Verify durable effects and committed progress using a real broker/database integration test.

questions.question: How do Kafka listener acknowledgments interact with database commits?
questions.answer: Acknowledge according to the durable effect you promise, not merely receipt or task submission. Committing progress before the database effect risks loss; committing after the effect leaves a duplicate window. Make the effect idempotent and verify partition ordering, redelivery and rebalance behavior. Kafka transactions alone do not make an external database write atomic with the offset.

questions.question: The listener submits work to an executor and returns. Has the record been processed?
questions.answer: only submission completed. Depending on the configured strategy, returning can allow progress before the task's durable effect. Track completion through the supported acknowledgment model.

questions.question: Record 11 finishes before record 10 in the same partition. Can you commit past both?
questions.answer: not safely if 10 is unfinished. A committed position describes a prefix of progress; advancing it can skip unfinished earlier work after restart. Preserve ordering or track a contiguous completed prefix through a supported design.

questions.question: A rebalance happens after a database commit but before acknowledgment. What prevents a double charge?
questions.answer: a durable unique operation key checked in the same database transaction as the charge. A process-local set is insufficient after restart or reassignment, and the key's retention must cover the redelivery horizon.

questions.question: How would you test Kafka progress across a rebalance?
questions.answer: stop the consumer before the effect, after commit and before acknowledgment; force reassignment; redeliver duplicates concurrently; and inject a poison record. Verify durable effects and committed progress using a real broker/database integration test.

groups.title: @Singleton, @Prototype and @Context processing
groups.mechanism: Micronaut's processors generate scope and construction metadata; the context controls actual object creation. Lazy defaults can be overridden by application startup configuration.
groups.tradeOff: Deferred creation improves startup selectivity while required misconfiguration may surface on first use.
groups.verify: Count actual constructions and closures under default and configured eager initialization.

questions.question: How does @Singleton work in Micronaut internally?
questions.answer: Compilation generates bean metadata carrying scope; runtime context resolution creates and reuses the scoped instance rather than constructing production objects during compilation.

questions.question: How does @Prototype differ from @Singleton?
questions.answer: Prototype resolution creates a new instance under its contract; singleton resolution reuses one scoped instance within the context.

questions.question: What does @Context change?
questions.answer: It requests context-lifecycle initialization instead of ordinary lazy singleton behavior, subject to the application's overall eager initialization configuration.

questions.question: Why can a singleton dependency fail only on first use?
questions.answer: Its actual creation may have been deferred, leaving runtime conditions, credentials or external resources unchecked during initial startup.

questions.question: How would you test scope annotations rather than their presence?
questions.answer: Resolve repeatedly through the actual context, compare identities and construction counts, then verify lifecycle cleanup and user-state isolation.

groups.title: @Factory, @Bean and @Inject metadata
groups.mechanism: Factory producers supply managed third-party objects through generated definitions. Injection resolves eligible types and qualifiers; direct factory calls remain ordinary calls unless explicitly mediated.
groups.tradeOff: Container ownership reduces manual assembly while scope and cleanup must be specified for produced clients.
groups.verify: Resolve clients by qualifier and verify created-instance counts plus resource closure.

questions.question: Why use @Factory for an SDK client?
questions.answer: It lets the container manage construction and injection of a third-party type that cannot conveniently carry application annotations.

questions.question: What does @Inject identify in Micronaut?
questions.answer: Supported constructor or member injection points represented in generated bean metadata and resolved by the application context.

questions.question: Does annotating a factory make every produced object a safe singleton?
questions.answer: No. The produced bean's declared scope and lifecycle contract must be reviewed independently from the factory's role.

questions.question: Why can the wrong Named import or qualifier break injection?
questions.answer: The metadata must express the qualifier recognized by the configured injection system; similar names do not establish equivalent contracts.

questions.question: How would you verify factory-produced client ownership?
questions.answer: Assert the selected qualifier, shared or per-lookup lifetime, bounded pool creation and exact shutdown behavior after context closure.

groups.title: @Requires and @Replaces eligibility
groups.mechanism: Requires expresses prerequisites for bean eligibility; Replaces intentionally substitutes a targeted definition. Generated metadata still leaves environment and candidate selection decisions for runtime.
groups.tradeOff: Flexible composition needs precise targets to avoid fake or unrelated implementations becoming eligible.
groups.verify: Start contexts with absent properties, competing qualifiers and replacement factories.

questions.question: How does @Requires differ from a Java if statement?
questions.answer: It governs container eligibility from condition metadata rather than branching inside an already created business object.

questions.question: How does @Replaces differ from @Primary?
questions.answer: Replaces targets substitution of a definition; Primary expresses selection preference among eligible candidates without universally deleting the others.

questions.question: Why can @Requires compile but disable a bean in production?
questions.answer: Conditions can depend on runtime properties, environments or available beans that differ from compilation and test environments.

questions.question: Why can a broad @Replaces declaration mask a wiring defect?
questions.answer: It can remove more candidates than intended or replace a different qualifier, making tests observe an unrealistic graph.

questions.question: How would you review a conditional replacement?
questions.answer: Document the target type, qualifier and factory where relevant, then test production and test configurations independently with explicit selected identities.

groups.title: @Around and @InterceptorBean internals
groups.mechanism: Around metadata declares interception behavior, and InterceptorBean associates an interceptor with bindings. Compile-time-generated proxies execute a runtime interceptor chain on eligible methods.
groups.tradeOff: Generated advice avoids some discovery work but method eligibility and proxy mode still affect semantics.
groups.verify: Count interceptor execution through external calls, self-calls and configured proxy-target behavior.

questions.question: What role does @InterceptorBean play?
questions.answer: It links a managed interceptor to supported interceptor binding annotations so generated advice can select it.

questions.question: How does @Around affect code generation?
questions.answer: It marks supported around-advice bindings that lead Micronaut's compilation infrastructure to generate interception machinery for eligible methods.

questions.question: Why can default Micronaut self-invocation differ from Spring proxy AOP?
questions.answer: Default subclass interception can receive eligible internal virtual calls, while ordinary Spring target self-calls bypass its external proxy.

questions.question: Why can a final or private method defeat a subclass-advice assumption?
questions.answer: Subclass proxies cannot override those methods in the needed way; verify the concrete supported advice and compilation diagnostics.

questions.question: How would you test a custom annotation interceptor?
questions.answer: Use the actual managed bean and binding, assert result and exception behavior, and test ordering plus bypass cases rather than direct interceptor construction alone.

groups.title: @Introspected and @Serdeable generation
groups.mechanism: Introspected provides generated bean-introspection metadata; Serdeable opts supported types into Micronaut Serialization. They serve related but different consumers.
groups.tradeOff: Generated metadata improves explicit support while serializer choice still determines wire behavior.
groups.verify: Round-trip a DTO through the configured serializer and inspect null, unknown and historical fields.

questions.question: What does @Introspected generate?
questions.answer: Compile-time bean introspection metadata enabling supported property and constructor access without ordinary runtime reflective discovery.

questions.question: What does @Serdeable declare?
questions.answer: Serialization and/or deserialization eligibility for the supported Micronaut Serialization integration, according to its annotation configuration.

questions.question: Why is @Introspected not a universal JSON contract?
questions.answer: The active serializer and its supported metadata determine wire behavior; introspection alone does not guarantee every serializer recognizes the type.

questions.question: Why can a DTO work with Jackson Databind but fail after switching serialization modules?
questions.answer: Supported annotations, constructors, polymorphism and opt-in rules can differ between integrations.

questions.question: How would you migrate serialization annotations safely?
questions.answer: Replay golden JSON with missing, null, unknown and old fields against both integrations and verify exact intended wire compatibility.

groups.title: @Controller, @Client and @ExecuteOn boundaries
groups.mechanism: HTTP annotation metadata describes server routes or client operations; ExecuteOn introduces a supported executor boundary. Transport dispatch and method advice remain distinct layers.
groups.tradeOff: Declarative interfaces reduce boilerplate but can conceal blocking, timeout and URI assumptions.
groups.verify: Exercise real routes and client calls while observing threads, deadlines and error mapping.

questions.question: How does @Controller with @Get expose a route?
questions.answer: Compilation supplies supported executable and route metadata used by the HTTP server to match requests and invoke the controller.

questions.question: What does @Client generate or configure?
questions.answer: A supported HTTP-client integration for annotated injection points or declarative interfaces, using configured transport and endpoint behavior.

questions.question: What does @ExecuteOn control?
questions.answer: The named executor boundary for supported execution, rather than converting a blocking operation into nonblocking I/O.

questions.question: Why can a controller's @ExecuteOn fail to protect an earlier blocking filter?
questions.answer: The filter runs at a distinct pipeline stage; moving the controller does not automatically relocate every other operation.

questions.question: How would you verify HTTP annotations end to end?
questions.answer: Test route methods, binding, media types, validation and client error outcomes, then inject dependency delay and confirm intended execution placement.
